catalog_locator: 'The Accent', p.7; immediate future tense, p.49
catalog_quote: THE ACCENT. The accent is invariably on the last syllable but one. When two vowels come together they are usually pronounced as close vowels, in which case the accent is thrown back to the first of these vowels, as ku-leiUiy [scanned-garbled example] to dun. When a suffix is used the accent is moved so as to be on the last syllable but one. There are but few monosyllabic words in the Sagalla dialect. ... [p.49] The immediate future is formed by the use of the same pronominal prefixes as in the mediate future, but without the syllable ./e- [scanned for je-], and slightly throwing the accent on the final syllable of the verb, as — ni-lima, I will cultivate. The final -a of this tense is often changed into -a^ga [scanned for -a'ga], as — ni-lim-a'gay [scanned for ni-lim-a'ga,] I will cultivate.

new_statements.translation: theses.fr English abstract: "We find a one end purely tonal systems (like kikuyu) and at the other end systems with purely demarcative penultimate stress, with all intermediate cases. [...] a hypothesis is presented according to which the emergence of penultimate accent is the main cause of the evolution of these systems."

The API record does say "accessible": "non" and the landing HTML has no full-text link, so the reader's account of theses.fr is accurate. BUT THE FULL TEXT IS OBTAINABLE: web.archive.org was reachable at (the reader hit a timeout); a CDX lookup for ddl.cnrs.fr/fulltext/Philippson* lists http://www.ddl.cnrs.fr:80/Fulltext/philippson…
new_statements.relation_note: The only text obtainable (the theses.fr abstract) does not mention Saghala/Taita, so it neither confirms nor contradicts the catalog's penultimate rule. Full text: theses.fr record marked not accessible; landing page has no full-text link; the Internet Archive's index and the DDL (ddl.cnrs.fr) site, where a copy might have been hosted, were both unreachable (connection timeout); two attempts made, no PDF obtained.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The abstract only says that the East African Bantu sample spans fully tonal languages (Kikuyu) to demarcative-penultimate-stress languages (Swahili) and that penultimate accent drove the diachrony; it does not name Sagalla/Saghala or say where its stress falls. The thesis body, where Saghala would be treated, could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: Catalog item is Sagalla = Saghala/Kisagalla (Guthrie E74b), sister of Davida/Dawida (E74a) within Taita (Odden 2006 p.33 wording: 'Mbololo is one of the dialects of Davida (E74a), a sister language of Saghala (E74b)'). Patin's work (2002 MA thesis, 2009 Faits de Langues) on the Teri dialect of Saghala remains unopened (paywalled/unheld per prior notes).

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Philippson 1991 (the only listed work; reader marked it silent on the basis of the abstract) DOES treat Saghala in the body: p.483 §3.5.2 (c) lists 'daβida et saghala' among 'langues à culmination de longueur, mais non de hauteur, sur la pénultième (langues à prosodèmes distinctifs, mais sans opposition de longueur)'; p.449 §2.7.3 says 'Le système tonal du saghala n'est pas encore bien connu, mais il semble avoir beaucoup de points communs avec celui du mijikenda' and that Saghala may be a marginal member of the north-east (Sabaki-type) group rather than Taita proper; p.72 places saghala (E 74b) in group XX (Taita) beside daβida (E 74a); p.515 states the data are Philippson's own field note…

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both deciding passages are verbatim in the held Wray 1894 djvu text at printed p.7 and p.49; the p.7 page image downloaded now confirms the wording and fixes the garbled example ('ku-leila, to dun'). (2) The classification rests on an 1894 SPCK missionary primer (pedagogical grammar/sketch) with an impressionistic, tone-blind 'accent' statement. For Sagalla proper Glottolog lists nothing better (2 refs: Wray 1894; unpublished Verbi & Austin notes), and repository searches (UoN, KU) found no Sagalla phonology thesis (the held UoN 2016 MA is a loanword study; its bibliography cites Mwasusu 2012 on Kidawida stress, a different language). However Breteler 2018's bibliography and Crossref show modern tone-focused fieldwork on Saghala by Patin (2002 MA thesis on the 'systeme accentuel'; 2009 Faits de Langues article), neither held nor open; held Breteler 2018 relays Patin's data
